title: Nasogastric tube placement
what: A thin, soft tube is passed through your nose into your stomach. It is used for feeding, giving medicines, or draining the stomach.
why: When a person cannot swallow or eat on their own, after some surgeries, for a bowel blockage, or for poisoning.
duration: placement usually takes 5 to 15 minutes; the tube stays as long as needed, from hours to weeks
tell_doctor: If you had a nose injury or surgery
If you have a disease of the food pipe

prepare.title: Prep
prepare.text: Usually no special prep. The nurse will explain what to do.

prepare.title: Signal
prepare.text: Agree on a hand signal you can use if you want to stop.

steps: You sit up with your head tilted slightly forward
The nurse measures how far the tube needs to go
The tip of the tube is coated with gel, and sometimes your nose is numbed
The tube is passed through a nostril
When it reaches your throat, you are asked to swallow. Small sips of water may help, if allowed
The tube position is checked, sometimes with an X-ray
The tube is taped to your nose
feel: It is unpleasant and may make you gag. Swallowing helps
While the tube is in, your throat may feel scratchy
after: Do not pull or move the tube yourself
The nurse checks your nose and the skin under the tape
If you go home with the tube, you will be taught how to feed and flush it
Removing the tube is quick and almost painless
red_flags: Coughing, choking, or trouble breathing during feeding: stop the feed and call the nurse right away or call emergency services
The tube has come out or moved: do not put it back yourself. Tell the nurse
A nosebleed that will not stop

faq.q: Can I talk with the tube in?
faq.a: Yes. The tube gets in the way a little, but you can talk.

faq.q: How long can the tube stay in?
faq.a: It depends on the reason. Usually a few days or weeks. If it is needed for longer, your doctor may suggest another method.

reminders.text: Your tube will be placed soon. Agree on a hand signal with the nurse in case you need a pause.
